content: The World Health Organization (WHO) published recommendations in 2013 regarding postnatal care for mothers and newborns. This document emphasizes the critical importance of the postnatal period, which encompasses the days and weeks following childbirth. This phase is vital for the health and well-being of both mothers and their newborns, as most maternal and infant deaths occur during this time. Despite its significance, the postnatal period is often neglected in terms of quality care provision. The recommendations were formulated through a rigorous process involving systematic reviews of evidence, expert consultations, and the use of the GRADE methodology to assess the quality of evidence and strength of recommendations. Key recommendations include: 1. Postnatal Care Timing and Frequency: For facility births, mothers and newborns should remain in the facility for at least 24 hours after delivery. For home births, the first postnatal contact should occur within 24 hours. Additional postnatal visits are recommended on day 3 (48–72 hours), between days 7–14, and at six weeks postpartum. 2. Home Visits: Home visits during the first week after birth are strongly recommended to provide care for both the mother and newborn. 3. Exclusive Breastfeeding: All infants should be exclusively breastfed from birth until six months of age. 4. Umbilical Cord Care: In settings with high neonatal mortality, the application of 4% chlorhexidine to the umbilical cord stump during the first week of life is recommended for home births. In low-mortality settings, clean and dry cord care is advised. 5. Newborn Care: Bathing should be delayed for at least 24 hours after birth (or at least six hours if cultural practices require earlier bathing). Newborns should be appropriately clothed, kept in the same room as their mothers, and encouraged to interact with their caregivers. Immunizations should follow existing WHO guidelines. 6. Maternal Assessment: During the first 24 hours postpartum, regular assessments of vaginal bleeding, uterine contraction, fundal height, temperature, and heart rate should be conducted. Urine voiding should be documented within six hours. Subsequent postnatal visits should assess general well-being, breastfeeding progress, emotional health, and signs of complications such as postpartum depression or domestic abuse. 7. Counseling: Women should receive information on the physiological recovery process, common health concerns, and when to seek medical attention. Counseling on nutrition, hygiene (especially handwashing), family planning, and safer sex practices is also recommended. In malaria-endemic areas, the use of insecticide-treated bed nets is advised. 8. Prophylactic Antibiotics: Antibiotics are recommended for women with thirdor fourth-degree perineal tears following vaginal delivery to prevent wound complications. 9. Psychosocial Support: Psychosocial support by trained personnel is recommended for women at high risk of postpartum depression. However, routine formal debriefing or distribution of educational materials for all women is not currently supported by sufficient evidence. The guidelines are intended for healthcare professionals, including physicians, midwives, nurses, and auxiliary nurse-midwives, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. They are also designed to assist policymakers, program managers, and educators in establishing and maintaining effective maternal and newborn care services. The recommendations will be regularly updated as new evidence becomes available, with major reviews occurring at least every five years.
